blocks.text: Design a notification service, the system responsible for taking one logical event, such as an order shipping or a suspicious login, and reliably reaching the affected user through one of several possible channels: push notification, SMS, or email. This is the first problem in this project's final category, Asynchronous Systems, and it introduces a fan-out shape genuinely different from the fan-out already covered elsewhere. Live comments and the news feed fan a single event out to many different users. This fans a single event out across multiple channels for one single user, gated by that user's own preferences, with automatic fallback if the preferred channel does not confirm delivery.
blocks.content: Design a notification service, the system responsible for taking one logical event, such as an order shipping or a suspicious login, and reliably reaching the affected user through one of several possible channels: push notification, SMS, or email. This is the first problem in this project's final category, Asynchronous Systems, and it introduces a fan-out shape genuinely different from the fan-out already covered elsewhere. Live comments and the news feed fan a single event out to many different users. This fans a single event out across multiple channels for one single user, gated by that user's own preferences, with automatic fallback if the preferred channel does not confirm delivery.

blocks.alt: One logical notification event is gated by the user's own per-channel preferences, then tried across channels in priority order, stopping the instant one confirms delivery, or honestly reporting undelivered if none do

blocks.text: The two techniques that define this design are per-user, per-channel preference gating with an urgency bypass, so a user's own opt-out choices are respected for ordinary messages but cannot silence a genuinely critical alert about their own account, and channel fallback with delivery confirmation, trying channels in priority order and stopping at the first one that genuinely confirms the message landed, rather than blindly firing at every channel at once.

blocks.text: A triggering event elsewhere in the platform should be able to request a notification be sent to a specific user, optionally marked urgent. The system should respect that user's own per-channel preferences for ordinary, non-urgent messages. A genuinely urgent notification should still reach the user through some channel, regardless of that user's opt-out preferences. The system should attempt delivery through channels in priority order, stopping as soon as one channel confirms the message actually landed. If no allowed channel confirms delivery, the system should honestly report the notification as undelivered rather than silently assuming success.

blocks.alt: Respecting each user's own channel preferences, still reaching the user for genuinely urgent events, avoiding notification fatigue, delivering time-sensitive notifications within seconds, and knowing definitively whether a notification actually landed

blocks.text: Respecting each user's own channel preferences means a user opting out of a channel for ordinary messages must genuinely stop receiving them there. Still reaching the user for urgent events means a security alert or other critical, account-affecting event should still reach the user through some channel, even one they have otherwise opted out of. Avoiding notification fatigue means many similar low-priority events arriving in a short window should collapse into a single digest rather than many separate, redundant pings. Delivering time-sensitive notifications quickly means an urgent notification needs its first delivery attempt to begin within a few seconds of the triggering event. And knowing definitively whether a notification landed means the sender needs a genuine, confirmed answer from the channel itself, not an optimistic assumption that firing a request was the same thing as delivering it.

items: What exactly counts as urgent enough to bypass a user's own channel preferences, and who decides that classification for a given event type?
Should the channel fallback order be fixed platform-wide, or configurable per event type, for example security alerts preferring SMS first while marketing preferring email first?
Is digesting and batching similar low-priority notifications in scope in depth, or can this design treat it as a later addition on top of the core delivery path?
What counts as a genuine delivery confirmation for each channel, a network-level acknowledgment from the provider, or an actual read receipt from the user?
Should a user be able to configure quiet hours during which even allowed channels defer non-urgent notifications until later?

blocks.text: This design assumes urgency is decided by the triggering event itself at the moment it requests a notification, based on a small, well-known set of event types classified as urgent, such as security alerts, rather than by any per-notification manual review. Delivery confirmation is assumed to mean a network-level acknowledgment from the channel's own provider that the message was accepted for delivery, not a full read receipt from the user, since requiring the latter would make honest, timely fallback impossible for channels like SMS that rarely offer one. Digesting and batching of low-priority notifications is assumed to be a layer that groups events before they ever reach the core preference-gating and fallback path described here, keeping that core path's logic simple and testable on its own.

blocks.text: A large platform can realistically trigger millions of individual notification events across a single busy day, with a widely relevant event, such as a platform-wide incident notice, capable of spiking a large burst of notifications within the very same minute. Urgent notifications specifically need their first delivery attempt to begin within a few seconds of the triggering event, since the entire point of urgency classification is timely reach.

blocks.text: A triggering event elsewhere in the platform reaches the notification service, which reads the affected user's own per-channel preferences to determine which channels are allowed for this particular message. The channel fallback router then tries those allowed channels in priority order, handing each attempt to that channel's own dedicated worker, push, SMS, or email, stopping the instant any one of them confirms delivery.

blocks.text: Each channel under consideration for a given notification is checked against that user's own stored preference for it. If the user has opted in, the channel is included among those this notification may use; if they have opted out and the message is not urgent, that channel is excluded entirely, never even attempted.

blocks.alt: A channel is allowed only if the user has opted into it, unless the message is urgent, in which case a channel the user opted out of is still excluded only from this specific gating step for non-urgent traffic

blocks.text: A genuinely urgent notification, such as a security alert about the user's own account, bypasses per-channel opt-out preferences entirely, every channel becomes eligible regardless of what the user has otherwise chosen. This exists specifically because a user should never be able to accidentally silence a critical alert about their own account simply by having opted out of routine notifications on a given channel.

blocks.text: Delivery is attempted through the highest-priority allowed channel first. If that channel confirms delivery, the process stops immediately, no further channels are tried. If it does not confirm, whether due to an outage, a rate limit, or simply an unreachable device, the request falls through to the next allowed channel in priority order, continuing until one confirms or the allowed channels are exhausted.

blocks.text: A user's channel preferences are modeled as a small, independently cacheable set of rows precisely because they are read on nearly every notification but change rarely, the opposite read-write ratio of the delivery attempt log, which is written constantly but read far less often, mostly for support and analytics. Every delivery attempt, confirmed or not, across every channel tried, is recorded, giving a complete, honest picture of exactly how a given notification was, or was not, ultimately delivered.

An urgent notification bypasses the user's own opt-out preferences entirely, falling through push and SMS before finally confirming on email, a channel the user had otherwise disabled

blocks.text: The happy path is the normal delivery flow above, a preference-filtered set of channels tried in order until one confirms. The workflow worth walking through separately is the urgent bypass, where the exact same fallback mechanism runs, but against a channel list unfiltered by the user's own preferences, this is deliberately the same code path with a different input, not a separate, parallel implementation, keeping the two behaviors consistent and easy to reason about together.

blocks.alt: A user's own channel preferences, read on nearly every notification, are cached with a short refresh so a recent preference change still takes effect promptly

blocks.text: Caching preference lookups aggressively is essential here, since they sit directly on the hot path of every non-urgent decision, but the cache is deliberately kept short-lived rather than indefinite, so a user who just opted out of a channel does not keep receiving it there for an extended period afterward.

blocks.alt: Every triggered notification event is routed into a separate queue per channel type, with each channel's own worker pool draining its queue independently

blocks.text: Separating channels into their own independent queues is what isolates one channel's own slowdown or outage, such as an SMS provider rate limit, from ever backing up delivery attempts for a completely unrelated channel like push.

blocks.alt: A notification allowed to use a given channel is load balanced across that channel's own independent worker pool, entirely separate from every other channel's pool

blocks.text: Each channel's worker pool is scaled and load balanced completely independently of every other channel's, since push, SMS, and email each have entirely different provider rate limits, latency characteristics, and failure modes.

blocks.alt: A single channel's queue depth growing faster than its own worker pool can drain triggers adding more workers to that one channel's pool independently

blocks.text: Scaling here means growing one specific channel's own worker pool in response to that channel's own observed load, never scaling all channels together as one undifferentiated unit, since their real-world bottlenecks are entirely unrelated to each other.

blocks.text: The preference store scales as a small, read-heavy dataset, easily replicated widely given how infrequently it changes relative to how often it is read. The delivery attempt log scales as an ordinary, append-heavy, time-partitioned log, similar in shape to this project's existing time-series design, read far more for later analysis than for any single live delivery decision.

blocks.alt: A user's own current channel preferences should be read reasonably fresh, since a stale read could send through a channel they just disabled; the historical delivery attempt log is only eventually consistent, fine for audit and analytics

blocks.text: Preference freshness matters because a stale read has a real, user-visible consequence, sending through a channel the user believed they had just turned off, while the delivery attempt log exists purely for audit and analytics and can lag without affecting any live decision.

blocks.alt: One channel's worker pool becoming fully unavailable is handled by the same fallback chain that handles an ordinary non-confirmation, continuing to the next allowed channel without the sender needing to know a whole channel was down

blocks.text: The fallback mechanism itself doubles as the reliability mechanism, a full outage of one channel's provider looks, from the fallback router's point of view, exactly like that channel simply failing to confirm every attempt, so no separate outage-handling logic is needed at all.

blocks.alt: An outgoing notification is only sent if it originates from a genuine, authenticated internal trigger; a forged or unauthenticated trigger is rejected before ever reaching a real user

blocks.text: Preventing notification spoofing, a malicious or compromised system triggering fake, convincing notifications, such as a fraudulent security alert used for phishing, is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since users are conditioned to trust and act on notifications that appear to come from the platform itself.

blocks.text: Per-channel confirmation rate is the most important thing to watch, a sudden drop for one specific channel signals a provider-side outage or rate-limit issue before it fully exhausts that channel's fallback capacity. The rate of notifications that exhaust every allowed channel without ever confirming is also worth tracking closely, since it directly measures how often users are genuinely not being reached at all.
blocks.content: Per-channel confirmation rate is the most important thing to watch, a sudden drop for one specific channel signals a provider-side outage or rate-limit issue before it fully exhausts that channel's fallback capacity. The rate of notifications that exhaust every allowed channel without ever confirming is also worth tracking closely, since it directly measures how often users are genuinely not being reached at all.

blocks.alt: A single channel provider having its own rate limit or outage, preference lookups on the hot path if not cached aggressively enough, and a single widely relevant event triggering an enormous simultaneous burst across all channels

blocks.text: Unlike several other designs in this project, none of these bottlenecks are structural single-writer requirements, they are ordinary capacity and dependency risks, each channel's own worker pool and provider relationship is the natural place to add resilience and headroom independently.

blocks.text: Preference gating combined with an urgency bypass and channel fallback is the right default because it is the only approach that respects a user's ordinary choices while still guaranteeing that a genuinely critical alert about their own account can never be accidentally silenced.

blocks.text: Stopping the fallback chain the instant any channel confirms delivery is itself a meaningful cost optimization, avoiding unnecessary sends through every remaining channel once the user has genuinely already been reached. Digesting and batching similar low-priority notifications before they reach the core delivery path further reduces total send volume across every channel, particularly for high-frequency, low-urgency event types.

items: A user has opted out of every single channel and a non-urgent notification is triggered for them, correctly resulting in the notification being honestly suppressed rather than forced through any channel.
A user has opted out of every channel but an urgent notification is triggered, correctly bypassing every opt-out and still attempting delivery across all channels.

A channel confirms delivery but the confirmation itself is delayed past when the next channel in the fallback chain was already attempted, correctly still recorded as a successful delivery on the first channel, with the redundant later attempt simply not needed.

A user updates their preferences at the exact moment a notification is being evaluated, correctly resolved by whichever preference state the read happened to observe, an acceptable, bounded staleness given the short cache refresh window.

blocks.text: A change to which event types are classified as urgent needs careful, deliberate review, since over-classifying routine events as urgent erodes the entire point of the preference system, while under-classifying a genuinely critical event risks a user never being reached about it. Per-channel confirmation rates deserve their own dedicated alerting, a silent, gradual drop in one channel's confirmation rate can go unnoticed far longer than an obvious, total outage would.

blocks.text: User-configurable quiet hours, deferring non-urgent notifications until a user-chosen time window even on an otherwise allowed channel, could be layered on top of this same preference-gating architecture as an additional filtering step. Smarter, adaptive channel ordering, learning per-user which channel has historically confirmed fastest for them rather than using one fixed, platform-wide priority order, would let the fallback chain reach most users on its very first attempt more often.

items: Architecture: per-user per-channel preference gating with an urgency bypass, paired with channel fallback that stops at the first confirmed delivery.
Capacity: a large platform triggering millions of notification events a day, with urgent notifications needing their first delivery attempt within a few seconds.
The core techniques: preference gating with an urgency bypass and channel fallback, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: a small, read-heavy, cacheable preference store alongside a durable, append-heavy delivery attempt log.
End-to-end workflows: a normal preference-filtered fallback flow and an urgent bypass flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: reasonably fresh preference reads on the hot path, paired with an eventually consistent delivery attempt log used only for audit and analytics.

Trade-offs: preference gating with an urgency bypass versus always sending through every channel versus strict preference respect with no bypass, compared directly on user trust and reach for critical events.
